[SPEAKER_01] Good morning everyone. I am pleased to present our work on the Lab Knowledge Container, or
[SPEAKER_01] LJC. This project focuses on the critical intersection of transit knowledge capture
[SPEAKER_01] and knowledge transfer systems. As many of you may know, the most valuable assets in
[SPEAKER_01] any research laboratory or industrial setting often resides in the
[SPEAKER_01] in the minds of its most experienced members. Our goal with LKC is to build a system that prevents
[SPEAKER_01] this expertise from evaporating when individuals leave an organization.
[SPEAKER_01] This research is led by Professor Shuoyuan Cho at the National Taiwan University of
[SPEAKER_01] Science and Technology, where we direct the Center for Internet of Things Innovation.
[SPEAKER_01] To understand the motivation behind LKC, we must first address the nature of passive knowledge.
[SPEAKER_01] Unlike explicit knowledge, which is easily codified in manuals or databases,
[SPEAKER_01] passive knowledge is deeply personal, experience-based, and difficult to articulate.
[SPEAKER_01] It is the know-how used in troubleshooting and decision-making.
[SPEAKER_01] Current research indicates that a staggering 74% of organizations lack formal processes for transferring this knowledge.
[SPEAKER_01] When an expert retires or moves on, the organization often faces a two-clocks problem,
[SPEAKER_01] losing both the static state

[SPEAKER_01] of information and the ephemeral reasoning behind it.

[SPEAKER_01] This model describes the continuous spiral of knowledge creation through four stages
[SPEAKER_01] – socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization.
